strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting human response times under changing external feedback. Using a learned controller to modulate evidence accumulation is a plausible and potentially useful combination of neural and cognitive modeling.

The two-day study provides repeated behavioral measurements from 36 retained participants across four initially randomized conditions, including a no-pressure control. This supplies useful empirical grounding for the modeling problem.

Evaluation includes individual, group, general, and leave-one-participant-out settings. The hybrid model achieves lower aggregate MAPE than Pure DRL in all four settings. The feature ablation and reported training-time reduction provide additional encouraging evidence.
weaknesses: Essential methodological details are missing from the supplied manuscript. Appendices S2–S6 are referenced but absent; the main text does not specify the RL algorithm and reward, diffusion dynamics and parameter construction, key hyperparameters, or adaptive feedback rule sufficiently for reproduction. It is also unclear whether all human-data-dependent stages, including SVM fitting and model selection, respect the participant holdouts. Promised code and data availability does not resolve these gaps. Source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b07/review-experiment-kvoduhnb/call-5cedd6e498ab418eb0193cf2fc0d0a6b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main comparison does not isolate the contribution of the cognitive model. Pure DRL changes temporal processing and action granularity alongside removing the DDM. Comparisons with a supervised temporal predictor using equivalent inputs, a feedback-conditioned regressor, and a time-varying diffusion model would establish whether the proposed combination is necessary. The claim that DDM is restricted to posterior estimation is also misleading: fitted diffusion models can generate prospective predictions. Consequently, the advance over existing cognitive/neural and RL–DDM combinations is insufficiently established.

The cognitive interpretation exceeds the evidence. Predicting endpoint response times does not establish that the learned within-trial trajectories recover human evidence accumulation; their identifiability and psychological validity are untested. Figure 3(p) even shows nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories in the no-pressure group, suggesting these trajectories can absorb baseline prediction errors. Independent process measurements, model-recovery experiments, or predictions under altered stimulus timing would substantially strengthen this central claim.

Predictive improvements are modest and lack uncertainty estimates for the differences: general-level MAPE changes from 0.3034 to 0.2999, and leave-one-participant-out MAPE from 0.3037 to 0.2905. Participant-level paired analyses and quantified training variability are needed to assess reliability. The reported runtime advantage is promising, but convergence criteria and tuning budgets are insufficiently specified.

The behavioral claim that random feedback provides the best regulation is stronger than the reported statistical evidence. The significant pairwise result is random versus no pressure, which does not establish superiority over the other feedback conditions. Only seven participants remain in the random group, and removing three participants as 'extreme outliers' without specifying the criterion or sensitivity analysis further limits confidence.

Smaller presentation issues hinder verification: Figure 3 is crowded, numerical comparisons rely heavily on radar plots, and the approximately 25,000-trial dataset is not clearly reconciled with the retained sample and exclusions. These are secondary to the methodological and evidential concerns driving the weak-reject recommendation.
